[Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces HRLI@K: how often the last history item appears among full-catalog top-K recommendations. Useful for detecting last-item copying, but unavailable after seen-item filtering and insufficient to establish harmful reliance on recent intent. [Recency-weighted pairwise probes (RecSys 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) outperform reproduced SASRec variants on several benchmarks, showing that strong recency signals can support accurate prediction without higher-order sequence modeling.

[A temporal-attribution benchmark (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27201) reports stronger faithfulness for Integrated Gradients and GradientSHAP than raw attention. Its separately trained, masking-robust probe addresses distribution shift from naive masking. This supports controlled interventions, while highlighting that perturbation sensitivity alone does not demonstrate generalization or causal user intent.

Design implication, rather than an established protocol from these papers: cross recency-residual enabled/disabled with recent/older-history interventions, keeping sequence length, occupied positions, positional embeddings, and attention masks fixed. Replace item embeddings in place; compare against equal-size random and popularity-matched controls. Separately vary positional inputs while holding item identities fixed. Measure paired target-rank changes, score-margin changes, and top-K overlap by category and history length; the difference between branch-enabled and branch-disabled intervention effects estimates branch dependence, including downstream interactions. Treat training-history results as sensitivity diagnostics. Select changes using the authorized macro validation HR@10; neither residual ablation nor high recent-history sensitivity alone establishes a harmful shortcut.
